cemc-pascal-2002-01.title: Evaluate
cemc-pascal-2002-01.body:
Numerator $15+9-6=18$, denominator $3\times2=6$, so the value is $\frac{18}{6}=3$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

cemc-pascal-2002-05.title: Net change
cemc-pascal-2002-05.body:
The net change is $+7-6+5=+6$ floors. She ended on floor 20, so she started on floor $20-6=14$.

**Answer: (A) 14**

cemc-pascal-2002-05.title: Work backwards
cemc-pascal-2002-05.body:
From 20, undo each move: down 5 to 15, up 6 to 21, down 7 to 14.

**Answer: (A) 14**

cemc-pascal-2002-06.title: Alternate angles
cemc-pascal-2002-06.body:
The angles of the triangle add to $180^\circ$, so the top angle is $180-70-50=60^\circ$. The line on the right is parallel to the left side of the triangle (the arrows), and the right side of the triangle crosses both. So $x$ and the top angle are alternate angles: $x=60$.

**Answer: (B) 60**

cemc-pascal-2002-06.title: Corresponding angles
cemc-pascal-2002-06.body:
The parallel line on the right makes the same angle with the base as the left side of the triangle: $70^\circ$ (corresponding angles). The angles along the base at the right vertex add to $180^\circ$: $50+x+70=180$, so $x=60$.

**Answer: (B) 60**

cemc-pascal-2002-09.title: Equal ratios
cemc-pascal-2002-09.body:
The rectangles 6 and 15 have the same height, so the left column is $\frac{6}{15}=\frac25$ as wide as the right column. The shaded rectangle has the same height as the 25 rectangle, so its area is $\frac25\cdot25=10$.

**Answer: (E) 10**

cemc-pascal-2002-09.title: Cross products
cemc-pascal-2002-09.body:
In such a grid the products of diagonally opposite areas are equal: $6\times25=15\times S$, so $S=\frac{150}{15}=10$. (For example, widths 2 and 5 with heights 3 and 5 give areas 6, 15, 10, 25.)

**Answer: (E) 10**

cemc-pascal-2002-10.title: Add three each time
cemc-pascal-2002-10.body:
Each new square needs 3 more toothpicks. Starting from 4 for one square, 10 squares need $4+9\times3=31$.

**Answer: (C) 31**

cemc-pascal-2002-10.title: Formula
cemc-pascal-2002-10.body:
Count 1 toothpick for the left end and 3 for each square (top, bottom, right side): $1+3\times10=31$.

**Answer: (C) 31**

cemc-pascal-2002-11.title: Sides are equal
cemc-pascal-2002-11.body:
$x+16=3x$, so $x=8$ and each side is $24$. The perimeter is $4\times24=96$.

**Answer: (C) 96**

cemc-pascal-2002-12.title: Find the first term
cemc-pascal-2002-12.body:
Let the first number be $a$. Then the list is $a, 2a, 4a, 8a, 16a, 32a$. From $2a+4a=24$, $a=4$, and the sixth number is $32\cdot4=128$.

**Answer: (E) 128**

cemc-pascal-2002-12.title: Use the second term
cemc-pascal-2002-12.body:
If the second number is $s$, the third is $2s$, so $3s=24$ and $s=8$. Doubling four more times: $16, 32, 64, 128$.

**Answer: (E) 128**

cemc-pascal-2002-13.title: Vertical base
cemc-pascal-2002-13.body:
$AC$ is vertical (both have $x=1$) with length $2-(-4)=6$. The height is the horizontal distance from $B$ to the line $x=1$: $4-1=3$. Area $=\frac12\cdot6\cdot3=9$.

**Answer: (E) 9**

cemc-pascal-2002-14.title: Total marks
cemc-pascal-2002-14.body:
The total is $25\cdot75+5\cdot40=1875+200=2075$. The class average is $\frac{2075}{30}\approx69.2$, closest to 69.

**Answer: (B) 69**

cemc-pascal-2002-14.title: Weighted shift
cemc-pascal-2002-14.body:
The 5 low students are $\frac16$ of the class and are 35 points below 75, so they pull the average down by $\frac{35}6\approx5.8$: $75-5.8\approx69.2$.

**Answer: (B) 69**

cemc-pascal-2002-15.title: Half the perimeter
cemc-pascal-2002-15.body:
By Pythagoras, $BC=\sqrt{120^2+160^2}=200$ m, so the perimeter is $480$ m. Together Jack and Jill cover the whole path, so each jogs $240$ m. Jack runs $160$ m from $A$ to $B$, then $240-160=80$ m from $B$ to $F$.

**Answer: (D) 80**

cemc-pascal-2002-15.title: Equation
cemc-pascal-2002-15.body:
Let $FB=x$. Then $CF=200-x$. Equal distances: $160+x=120+(200-x)$, so $2x=160$ and $x=80$.

**Answer: (D) 80**

cemc-pascal-2002-16.title: Odd times 5
cemc-pascal-2002-16.body:
$7^{52}$ is odd, and $5^3=125$. An odd number times a number ending in 5 ends in 5.

**Answer: (A) 5**

cemc-pascal-2002-16.title: Units digits
cemc-pascal-2002-16.body:
$7^{52}$: powers of 7 end in $7,9,3,1$ repeating; $52$ is a multiple of 4, so $7^{52}$ ends in 1. Then the product ends in the last digit of $5\cdot1=5$.

**Answer: (A) 5**

cemc-pascal-2002-17.title: Separate the 2s and 5s
cemc-pascal-2002-17.body:
$1000=2^3\cdot5^3$. If one factor had both a 2 and a 5, it would be a multiple of 10 and end in 0. So the factors are $2^3=8$ and $5^3=125$, and $8+125=133$.

**Answer: (C) 133**

cemc-pascal-2002-17.title: List factor pairs
cemc-pascal-2002-17.body:
Factor pairs of 1000: $1\times1000, 2\times500, 4\times250, 5\times200, 8\times125, 10\times100, 20\times50, 25\times40$. Only $8\times125$ has no zeros. Sum $133$.

**Answer: (C) 133**

cemc-pascal-2002-18.title: Add all three
cemc-pascal-2002-18.body:
Adding the three sums counts each person twice: $2(A+J+R)=280$, so $A+J+R=140$. Since $J+R=88$, $A=140-88=52$.

**Answer: (D) 52**

cemc-pascal-2002-18.title: Substitute
cemc-pascal-2002-18.body:
From the first two, $J-R=101-91=10$. With $J+R=88$, $J=49$ and $R=39$. Then $A=101-49=52$.

**Answer: (D) 52**

cemc-pascal-2002-19.title: Multiples of 7
cemc-pascal-2002-19.body:
Column 7 contains the multiples of 7, and row $n$ ends with $7n$. Since $2002=7\cdot286$, 2002 is in column 7, row 286. So $m+n=7+286=293$.

**Answer: (D) 293**

cemc-pascal-2002-19.title: Division with remainder
cemc-pascal-2002-19.body:
The number $k$ is in row $\lceil k/7\rceil$ and column given by its remainder on division by 7 (remainder 0 means column 7). $2002\div7=286$ exactly, so row 286, column 7: $m+n=293$.

**Answer: (D) 293**

cemc-pascal-2002-20.title: Try each x
cemc-pascal-2002-20.body:
We need $25-x^2\ge0$, so $-5\le x\le5$, and $25-x^2$ must be a perfect square. $x=0$: 25 ✓; $x=\pm3$: 16 ✓; $x=\pm4$: 9 ✓; $x=\pm5$: 0 ✓; $x=\pm1$: 24 ✗; $x=\pm2$: 21 ✗. That gives 7 values.

**Answer: (A) 7**

cemc-pascal-2002-20.title: Lattice points on a circle
cemc-pascal-2002-20.body:
If $\sqrt{25-x^2}=y\ge0$, then $x^2+y^2=25$. The integer solutions with $y\ge0$ are $(0,5),(\pm3,4),(\pm4,3),(\pm5,0)$: 7 values of $x$.

**Answer: (A) 7**

cemc-pascal-2002-21.title: Largest cube that fits
cemc-pascal-2002-21.body:
The block has volume $4\cdot5\cdot6=120$ cm$^3$. The largest cube we can leave has side 4 (the smallest dimension), volume 64. So at least $120-64=56$ cubes must be removed.

**Answer: (E) 56**

cemc-pascal-2002-21.title: Check the choices
cemc-pascal-2002-21.body:
Removing $n$ cubes leaves $120-n$, which must be a perfect cube no bigger than $4^3$: $64, 27, 8, 1$. The smallest $n$ is $120-64=56$.

**Answer: (E) 56**

cemc-pascal-2002-22.title: Inclusion–exclusion
cemc-pascal-2002-22.body:
$500-40=460$ students voted in favour of at least one issue. So $375+275-\text{both}=460$, giving both $=190$.

**Answer: (C) 190**

cemc-pascal-2002-22.title: Venn diagram
cemc-pascal-2002-22.body:
Let $b$ vote for both. Only the first: $375-b$; only the second: $275-b$. Then $(375-b)+(275-b)+b+40=500$, so $690-b=500$ and $b=190$.

**Answer: (C) 190**

cemc-pascal-2002-23.title: Write 64 as a power
cemc-pascal-2002-23.body:
$64=2^6=4^3=8^2=64^1$, and with an even exponent the base may also be negative: $(-2)^6=(-8)^2=64$. So the pairs are $(64,1),(8,2),(-8,2),(4,3),(2,6),(-2,6)$. (A zero or negative exponent cannot give 64 with an integer base.) That is 6 pairs.

**Answer: (D) 6**

cemc-pascal-2002-23.title: Go through exponents
cemc-pascal-2002-23.body:
$b$ must be positive (for $b\le0$, $a^b$ is 1, undefined or a fraction of absolute value at most 1). $b$ must divide 6 since $64=2^6$: $b=1$: $a=64$; $b=2$: $a=\pm8$; $b=3$: $a=4$; $b=6$: $a=\pm2$. Total 6.

**Answer: (D) 6**

cemc-pascal-2002-24.title: Semicircle minus segment
cemc-pascal-2002-24.body:
$AB=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$, so semicircle $AEB$ has radius $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and area $\frac12\pi\cdot\frac12=\frac\pi4$. The part of it inside the original circle is the segment between chord $AB$ and arc $AB$: quarter circle $AOB$ minus $\triangle AOB$, i.e. $\frac\pi4-\frac12$. The shaded area is $\frac\pi4-\left(\frac\pi4-\frac12\right)=\frac12$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{1}{2}$**

cemc-pascal-2002-24.title: Lune of Hippocrates
cemc-pascal-2002-24.body:
Let $S$ be the segment between chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$ of the original circle. Then shaded $+\,S$ is semicircle $AEB$, of area $\frac\pi4$, and $S+\triangle AOB$ is the quarter circle $AOB$, also of area $\frac\pi4$. So the shaded area equals the area of $\triangle AOB=\frac12\cdot1\cdot1=\frac12$ — no $\pi$ at all.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{1}{2}$**

cemc-pascal-2002-25.title: The moment water starts pouring in
cemc-pascal-2002-25.body:
Water overflows the large container while the small container sinks, and the level stays at the rim, 20 cm. Water starts to pour into the small container when the small container's rim reaches 20 cm, i.e. when its bottom is 2 cm above the bottom of the large container. At that moment the water in the large container fills a full cylinder of height 2 below the small container plus the ring between them up to 20 cm:
$$\pi(6^2)(2)+\pi(6^2-5^2)(18)=72\pi+198\pi=270\pi.$$
From then on no more water is lost. At the end the small container sits on the bottom with its rim at 18 cm, so the ring holds water up to 18 cm: $11\pi\cdot18=198\pi$. The rest, $270\pi-198\pi=72\pi$, is inside the small container, at depth $\frac{72\pi}{25\pi}=2.88$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 2.88 cm**

cemc-pascal-2002-25.title: Track the lost water
cemc-pascal-2002-25.body:
Originally there is $36\pi\cdot17=612\pi$ cm$^3$. The large container overflows until the small one's bottom reaches 2 cm, at which point the water volume is $36\pi\cdot20$ minus the submerged part of the small container, $25\pi\cdot18$: $720\pi-450\pi=270\pi$. The final state has $198\pi$ in the ring (height 18) and the rest, $72\pi$, in the small container: depth $72/25=2.88$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 2.88 cm**
